courses.title: Build Your First AI Agent
courses.tagline: Orbit Outdoor's support team is drowning: 400 tickets a day, most of them "where is my order?". Their FAQ chatbot can talk, but it can't look anything up. Over six modules you build Scout, an AI agent that reads the question, calls the right tools, remembers the conversation and knows when to hand over to a person.
courses.goal: Design, build, test and deploy a working AI agent in Python: a language model that plans, calls tools, uses memory and stays inside safe limits.
learn: Explain what makes an agent different from a chatbot or a fixed workflow, and when each one is the right tool.
Call a language model from Python with a clear system prompt and get back structured JSON you can trust.
Give an agent tools, let it decide when to use them, and handle the errors real APIs throw.
Add memory, retrieval and a think-act-observe loop, then test, evaluate, guard and deploy the agent you built.

modules.title: Introduction to AI Agents
modules.pain: Orbit's FAQ chatbot apologised 400 times on Monday. It could talk about orders, but it couldn't look one up.

lessons.title: What is an AI agent?
notes: An AI agent uses a language model to decide its own next steps, and takes actions with tools until it reaches a goal.
Every agent runs the same loop: perceive what is in front of it, decide the next step, act, then look at the result.
Autonomy is a dial, not a switch: give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you trust it.

lessons.title: Agents vs. chatbots vs. workflows
notes: A chatbot replies with text, a workflow follows steps a person wrote in advance, and an agent decides its own steps as it goes.
If you can write the steps down ahead of time, a fixed workflow is usually cheaper, faster and easier to trust than an agent.
Use an agent when the steps depend on the request and need lookups and judgement; many jobs don't need one.

lessons.title: Real-world use cases of AI agents
notes: Agents already do real work in customer support, coding, research and operations, usually with a person checking what matters.
A good first agent job is repetitive, needs lookups to answer, and has mistakes that are easy to spot and cheap to fix.
Start with one narrow job and add the next only when the last one works reliably; that is how Scout grows in this course.

lessons.title: Core components: LLM, tools, memory, planning
notes: An agent has four core parts: a language model that decides, tools that act, memory that keeps context, and planning that orders the steps.
For tools you define, the model only asks; your code runs the tool and sends the result back, so your code has the final say.
You will build the parts in order: the model in Module 2, tools in Module 3, memory and planning in Module 4.

lessons.title: Setting up your development environment
notes: Use Python 3.11 or newer, with one virtual environment per project so its packages stay separate.
Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in code, and never commit it to Git.
A model call is a client, the messages create method and the text block from the reply; keep a messages list and you have a chatbot that remembers.

modules.title: LLM Foundations for Agents
modules.pain: Scout's first draft promised a customer a 90-day refund. Orbit's policy is 30 days.
modules.lead_in: You know what an agent is made of. Now you get to know its brain: how a language model produces text, how to pick one, and how to instruct it so it answers in a shape your code can use.

lessons.title: How large language models work
notes: A language model writes by predicting the next token, adding it and repeating; a token is about three quarters of a word.
The model sees only what is in its context window and keeps nothing between requests, so your code sends the whole conversation every time.
It sounds just as sure when it is wrong, so give it the facts and rules it needs instead of leaving gaps for it to fill.

lessons.title: Choosing a model and API setup
notes: Weigh each step on quality, speed and cost; output tokens cost five times as much as input tokens.
Start with the most capable model, measure, then move simple high-volume steps to a cheaper model once tests show quality holds.
A request names the model, a max_tokens ceiling, the system prompt and the messages; the reply's text sits in a list of content blocks.

lessons.title: Prompt engineering essentials
notes: Most bad answers come from missing information, not missing magic words: be specific and give the model the facts.
Examples teach style fastest, and naming the format tells the model exactly what shape to answer in.
Break big tasks into steps, test prompts on real emails, and fix one gap at a time.

lessons.title: System prompts and role design
notes: The system prompt is the agent's job description: role, goal, rules, tone, facts and what to do when unsure.
Give the real facts and a reason for each rule, and the model stays inside policy even when a customer pushes.
Never put secrets in a prompt: keys live in environment variables and permissions live in code.

lessons.title: Structured outputs (JSON, schemas)
notes: When code reads the answer, ask for JSON, not prose: a JSON schema fixes the fields, their types and the allowed values.
Pass the schema in output_config, or use Pydantic with messages.parse, and the reply comes back in that shape.
A valid shape is not a true answer: check the stop reason and the values, and route anything odd to a person.

modules.title: Giving Your Agent Tools
modules.pain: Scout told a customer her parcel was delivered. The tracking service had timed out, and Scout filled the gap with a guess.
modules.lead_in: Your model can now follow instructions and answer in JSON. Next it gets hands: tools it can call to look things up and do things, and the code that keeps those calls safe when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: What is tool calling?
notes: A model can't run code or reach your systems; it can only ask for a tool by name, with arguments.
Your code runs the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result, matched to the request by its id.
Tool calling is a cycle: the model asks, your code runs, the result returns, and the model answers or asks again.

lessons.title: Defining and registering tools
notes: A tool definition has three parts: a name, a description, and an input_schema that describes its arguments.
The description is a prompt: say what the tool does, when to use it, what input looks like and what it returns.
Registering a tool means passing the TOOLS list on every request and mapping each name to a Python function.

lessons.title: Building tools: web search, calculator, file access
notes: Web search can be a server tool: add web_search to the tools list and Anthropic runs it, returning results with sources.
Models are unreliable at exact arithmetic, so give them a calculator that parses with ast and never calls eval.
A file tool opens files only inside one allowed folder, and refuses paths like ../ that climb out of it.

lessons.title: Connecting external APIs
notes: Wrap an external API in a thin function with a clear name, like track_parcel, and define it as a tool.
API keys live in your code's environment, never in the prompt, and every call gets a timeout.
Slow down when the API answers 429, and return only the fields the model needs, not the whole response.

lessons.title: Handling tool errors and edge cases
notes: When a tool fails, send back a tool_result with is_error true and a clear message, so the model can recover.
Never swallow an error into an empty string: the model reads silence as success and fills the gap with a guess.
Retry temporary failures with backoff, cap the loop with a step limit, and when stuck, tell the customer honestly or hand off.

modules.title: Memory, Planning and Reasoning
modules.pain: Twenty messages into a chat, Scout asked Ravi for his order number again. He had given it in the second message.
modules.lead_in: Scout can now use tools. Next it learns to remember what matters, look up the right facts, break a big request into steps, and keep thinking, acting and checking until the job is done.

lessons.title: Short-term vs. long-term memory
notes: A model remembers nothing between calls; your code decides what it sees each time.
Short-term memory is this conversation's messages; long-term memory is what you save and load later, like preferences and past orders.
Store the least data that does the job: never payment details, and no personal data you don't need.

lessons.title: Managing conversation context
notes: The context window is large, but every token you send costs money and time, and every call resends the chat.
Keep long chats lean: trim old turns, summarise what you trim, and pin key facts like the order number.
Trim at whole customer turns, so a tool call is never separated from its result.

lessons.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) basics
notes: RAG means retrieve the relevant chunks, add them to the prompt, and generate the answer from them.
Keyword scoring is a simple start; embeddings in a vector store such as Chroma or pgvector match meaning, not just words.
Answer only from retrieved text, say so when it doesn't cover the question, and keep your sources current.

lessons.title: Planning and task decomposition
notes: Task decomposition splits one request into small steps, each a tool call or a reply.
Plan first: a short list of steps written before acting keeps a multi-step request on track.
When a step fails, re-plan with what you learned instead of pushing on or giving up.

lessons.title: The agent loop: think, act, observe (ReAct)
notes: ReAct, short for reason and act, is the agent loop: think, act, observe, and repeat until the job is done.
Your code runs the loop and the tools; the model decides each step, and a trace shows why.
Every loop needs a step limit in code, and an honest hand-off with a summary when it is reached.

modules.title: Build Your First Agent (Hands-on Project)
modules.pain: Scout's first full test run: 38 of 60 answers right. Black Friday is three weeks away.
modules.lead_in: You have every part. Now you put them together: scope Scout properly, build it piece by piece, connect its tools and memory, then test and measure it until the numbers say it is ready.

lessons.title: Project scoping and architecture design
notes: Scope an agent to one job done well, and write down what it will not do and who handles that instead.
Decide how you will measure success before you build: a pass rate target, zero policy breaks and zero invented facts.
Draw the architecture first: the customer, the agent loop, tools, data, memory, a trace and a path to a person.

lessons.title: Building the agent step by step
notes: Start with the smallest loop that runs, then add one tool or feature at a time.
After every change, run Scout on a real question and read the trace before moving on.
When something breaks, the cause is almost always the last piece you added.

lessons.title: Adding tools and memory to the project
notes: Scout has six tools: four that look things up and two that act, with the rules for acting built into the tool.
Fake data in data/orders.json lets you test every hard case, from a late return to a carrier timeout, without real systems.
Memory keeps the recent turns plus pinned facts, like the order ID and email, that are never trimmed.

lessons.title: Testing and debugging the agent
notes: A trace records every step of a run: the tool Scout chose, the input it sent and the result or error that came back.
To debug, reproduce the failing case, read the trace from the top and fix the first bad step; later mistakes often follow from it.
Most agent bugs are one of four: wrong tool, wrong arguments, an ignored tool error, or a loop.

lessons.title: Evaluating agent performance
notes: A test set is real customer questions with expected outcomes, run the same way every time so scores can be compared.
Check every answer for the right tool, the key facts, policy kept and nothing invented, and track the pass rate after every change.
Read the failures, not just the number: good enough to ship means the failures left are safe.

modules.title: Deployment and Next Steps
modules.pain: A test copy of Scout looped on a failing tool all weekend. On Monday, the bill was $1,800.
modules.lead_in: Scout works on your machine. The last step is making it safe, affordable and reachable: guardrails, limits and monitoring, a real endpoint, and a look at what comes after one agent.

lessons.title: Safety, guardrails and responsible AI
notes: Guardrails are checks in your own code, layered around the agent: input checks, step and spend limits, approval for risky actions, output checks and logging.
Text from customers, web pages and documents is data, never instructions, even when it says to ignore your rules.
Tell customers they are talking to an AI, protect their personal data, and always offer a way to reach a person.

lessons.title: Cost, latency and monitoring
notes: Cost is tokens times price, and every step re-sends the whole conversation, so each step costs more than the last.
Cut cost with shorter prompts, trimmed history, smaller models for simple steps, step limits and prompt caching; cut waiting with fewer steps and streaming.
Log tokens, cost, latency, tool errors and hand-offs for every request, and set alerts before a bill surprises you.

lessons.title: Deploying the agent (web app or API)
notes: Deploying means wrapping Scout in an API endpoint, such as POST /chat, so a website or app can send a message and get a reply.
The API key stays on the server, in an environment variable; never in a browser, an app or your code.
Each chat sends a session id, so the server can keep that customer's conversation separate from everyone else's.

lessons.title: Intro to multi-agent systems and frameworks
notes: When one agent has too many tools or jobs, split the work into specialist agents with a coordinator that routes each request.
More agents mean more model calls, more cost and more places to break, so start with one and split only when tests show it struggling.
Frameworks and SDKs such as Anthropic's tool runner, LangGraph, CrewAI or a managed agent platform give you the loop, tools and memory ready-made.

lessons.title: Course recap and next learning path
notes: Scout now reads a question, plans, calls tools, remembers, follows policy, hands off when it should and runs behind an API with limits.
Good next steps are evaluations at scale, retrieval with embeddings, more tools through MCP, and multi-agent systems.
Next in the course: the mini project, where you ship Scout end to end, then the final assessment and a short reflection.
